stages.name: National wellbeing
stages.title: National wellbeing
stages.sub: Why the ONS looks beyond personal feelings to judge a nation's wellbeing, and how this data is used alongside GDP.

steps.q: Two people report the same happiness and health scores. One lives somewhere with a good local school and green parks, the other doesn't. Do they have the same quality of life?
steps.wrong: Yes, feelings are all that matter
steps.hint: Personal wellbeing covers how you feel inside. What about the world around you?
steps.pre: So beyond personal feelings, the ONS also has to look at

steps.q: To capture that surrounding picture, the ONS tracks things like people's jobs and activities, their local area, their money situation, the wider economy, their schooling, and the state of the environment. Are these about how a person feels, or about the conditions they live in?
steps.hint: Health and relationships are feelings-based. Jobs, area, money and environment are not.

steps.q: GDP can rise while pollution gets worse and commutes get longer, with none of that showing up in the GDP figure. What is missing from GDP alone?
steps.right: Information about living conditions and quality of life
steps.hint: GDP counts output, not the conditions people actually experience day to day.

steps.q: A government sees GDP growing but the wellbeing data showing falling personal finance scores and worsening local environments. Should it still assume everything is improving, or check the fuller picture before deciding on policy?
steps.right: Check the fuller picture before deciding
steps.hint: GDP alone missed the gap. What should sensible policymaking do with the extra data?
